opus-5.5.text:
The core problem with edge cases is that they're rare by definition. When Cruise was running driverless in San Francisco, the vehicles handled the everyday situations well: intersections, pedestrians, double-parked cars. The incidents that drew attention were things like emergency scenes with fire hoses across the road, unusual construction layouts, people behaving unpredictably, and situations where a pedestrian ends up somewhere no one expected. You might see one of those once in hundreds of thousands of miles, or not at all.

If you rely only on real-world driving data, you have to wait for those moments to happen, hope your sensors captured them well, and then label them. That's slow and expensive, and with safety-critical cases, waiting for them to happen on public roads isn't really acceptable.

Synthetic data changes that. Once you've seen one instance of a rare scenario, or even just imagined it, you can generate thousands of variations: different lighting, weather, angles, object positions, and agent behaviors. You're no longer limited by what the fleet happened to encounter. You can systematically explore the long tail instead of stumbling into it.

There's also the labeling advantage. In a simulated or generated scene you already know the ground truth exactly, where every object is, its depth, and its motion. With real data, getting that level of annotation for strange, cluttered scenes is very hard and error-prone.

Synthetic data doesn't replace real data. The distribution gap matters, and if your generated scenes don't look or behave like reality, the model learns the wrong things. But as generative models have gotten much better at producing realistic sensor data and plausible behavior, synthetic data has become the most practical way to cover the cases that actually decide whether the public trusts a driverless car. Average performance is largely solved. The tail is where these systems succeed or fail, and synthetic data is the tool built for the tail.

r002.rationale: The response says synthetic data enables systematic exploration of rare scenarios, but does not explain that this reveals additional system-level safety issues.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is that San Francisco is a city that produces situations you simply cannot plan for. A delivery truck double-parked on a hill, a fire truck trying to squeeze past, a pedestrian who steps out from behind a bus at the exact wrong moment, and then all three of those things happening at once in the fog. Cruise drove millions of miles there, and the problem was never the ordinary miles. The problem was the one-in-ten-million event. You could drive for years and still never collect enough real examples of a specific rare scenario to train or validate against it with any confidence.

That's where synthetic data changes the economics. If you've built a good enough simulation of the city, with realistic sensor noise, realistic agent behavior, realistic weather, you can take that one scary scenario you saw once and turn it into ten thousand variations. Move the pedestrian half a meter. Change the lighting. Add a second vehicle. Suddenly you're not waiting for the world to hand you the edge case again, you're manufacturing the long tail on demand.

The other piece is that the most important edge cases are, by definition, the ones you don't want to collect in real life. You cannot go out and stage a child running into the road to get training data. So synthetic data isn't just cheaper, it's the only ethical way to cover a whole class of safety-critical scenarios.

Now, I'll add the caveat, because it matters. Synthetic data only helps if the distribution is close enough to reality that the model's behavior transfers. If your simulator is too clean, you end up with a car that's brilliant in the simulator and confused on Market Street. So the real work is in closing that gap, and in being disciplined about using real-world incidents to seed and ground the synthetic scenarios, rather than just generating things that look plausible to an engineer. When Cruise ran into trouble, a lot of what people learned from it was exactly that lesson: the edge cases that hurt you are the ones your simulation didn't know to imagine.

astra-6.text:
The value is that those edge cases are precisely the situations you don’t encounter often enough to learn from reliably. You can collect a lot of driving data and still have very few examples of a particular unusual interaction.

Synthetic data lets you construct that situation and vary it: change the lighting, move an obstacle, or adjust when a pedestrian steps into the street. Then you can explore whether the system handles a whole range of related scenarios, rather than just the one example you happened to record.

But realism matters. If your simulation leaves out the thing that makes the situation difficult, you can get a false sense of confidence. So I see synthetic data as a complement to real-world data: use actual failures to guide what you generate, and validate that the improvements carry over to the real world.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that an edge case can be rare in the data but still matter enormously for safety. In a city like San Francisco, you can have unusual street layouts, construction, pedestrians, and vehicles interacting in combinations you haven’t seen before. Collecting more miles doesn’t guarantee you’ll capture the particular situation you need to understand.

Synthetic data lets you create variations of those situations in a controlled environment. You can change an actor’s position, timing, or behavior and test where the system starts to struggle, without exposing people to risk.

But its value depends on realism. If the simulation misses something important about the real world, good performance there can give you false confidence. So I see synthetic data as a way to target gaps in training and testing, alongside real-world data and validation.

r001.rationale: The response says rare edge cases can matter greatly for safety, but it does not identify their impact on autonomous-driving visual perception.

r002.rationale: It describes using synthetic variations alongside real-world data to test where the system struggles and target training and testing gaps, communicating how synthetic data can reveal safety issues.
